source.title: Superposition disentanglement of neural representations reveals hidden alignment
source.authors: André Longon; D. Klindt; Meenakshi Khosla

page_placements.theme: Cross-seed and cross-model universality is linked to unit interpretability

record.tranche_reason: Tests the superposition explanation in toy networks by comparing representations from differently initialized, capacity-limited models and examining whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) improve alignment. The real-network experiments extend this test but do not directly verify the networks’ superposition arrangements.
record.gate_note: The study examines sparse features packed into toy networks and measures alignment before and after SAE disentanglement. It does not test the cited InceptionV1 neuron, the prevalence of polysemantic neurons in language models, or whether that neuron has a shared feature. Alignment values shown only in figures are recorded as figure only. Cited results from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study takes the superposition hypothesis as a premise and uses it to ask whether differing superposition arrangements deflate alignment metrics. Its toy models are built to exhibit superposition (F=64 sparse features, N<F neurons, following Elhage et al.), so superposition is induced by design rather than tested as the cause of polysemanticity. The DNN results are explicitly unverified with respect to superposition; the authors say SAEs might be 'constructing new representations'. No row measures how many neurons are polysemantic, what causes it, or how it varies with architecture or measurement. All findings concern representational alignment, a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that differing superposition arrangements deflate predictive-mapping alignment, and that disentanglement is necessary to uncover true alignment. Gains appear in toy models, deep DNN layers and DNN→brain regression. Caveats: SAE→SAE regression mostly underperforms, and the effect in real DNNs cannot be verified as superposition per se.
record.recipe_differences: Uses TopK sparse autoencoders to transform representations and tests soft-matching and ridge-regression alignment; it does not reproduce the original neuron-level mixed-response analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Soft-matching effects varied by model size and layer: N=8 toy models decreased while N=16 and N=32 increased; ResNet50 decreased at the intermediate layer and increased at the deep layer, while ViT-B/16 increased at both tested layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Toy models with different seeds place the same shared features in different superposition arrangements. Almost all neurons have maximum semi-matching correlation below 0.5 across seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Identically designed networks trained from different seeds arrange superposed features differently across neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing neurons with SAE latents raises cross-seed soft-matching alignment at N=16 and N=32 toy sizes, at ResNet50 deep layers and at both ViT layers. It lowers alignment at N=8 and at ResNet50 layer2.3. It also raises SAE→Neuron regression scores and DNN→brain predictivity (ResNet50 +13.9%, ViT +3.5%), but SAE→SAE regression underperforms except at N=32.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition disentanglement with SAEs reveals hidden representational alignment between networks and with brains, depending on layer, model and metric.

record.problems: The authors cannot directly verify superposition arrangements in full-scale DNNs and acknowledge that SAEs may construct new representations. DNN-to-DNN and DNN-to-brain results are limited, the reported brain results emphasize one subject with the remaining subjects shown in a figure, and most alignment values are figure-only in the supplied text. SAE limitations include feature consistency, absorption, and identifiability.
record.rows_left_out: No separate semi-matching result from Appendix A.4 was extracted because it is described as highly consistent with the soft-matching results and its values are figure-only. The feature-to-neuron versus feature-to-SAE validation in Appendix A.3 was not included as a row because it validates SAE recovery rather than measuring the claim's neuron-level polysemanticity or its alignment outcome.

untested.parts: No measurement of mixed responses in image-classifier neurons. ResNet50 and ViT are studied only through alignment scores.
Superposition is imposed by the toy design (F>N, sparse features) and assumed for the DNNs. No test of whether it causes polysemantic neurons.
Polysemanticity under sufficient capacity is not examined.
The share of polysemantic neurons is not measured across activation functions, architectures or regularization, and no performance cost is reported.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: The study treats superposition as the premise of an alignment-metrics investigation, not as a claim under test. The reader's V3 labels are dropped: the toy models induce superposition by construction, and the semi-matching rows show arrangement diversity across seeds, not that superposition causes polysemanticity. The depth-dependent ResNet pattern is offered as consistent with superposition, but the authors acknowledge it is unverified.

versions.untested_parts: No test of mixed responses in image-classifier neurons or of the cited InceptionV1 neuron.
No language models or token/context response measurements.

Direct evidence is from toy networks with imposed sparse features and fewer neurons than features. The study cannot directly verify the superposition arrangements or causal mechanism in full-scale DNNs.
Does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.

Although it compares architectures and layers, it does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons or compare activation functions or regularization. It does not report the performance cost of reducing that share.
Does not investigate whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect one shared feature or related offshoots.
Does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

relation.reason: Superposition is a premise and the toy models are built to exhibit it. The paper does not test whether superposition causes polysemanticity.

tranche.reason: SAEs are used as a tool on a premise of superposition. The paper reports its own alignment-metric results, and the seed-arrangement result does not test a polysemanticity version. T2 (the reader's call) is arguable but not better.

source_check.notes: Rows r1-r3 are figure-only per size. The text states one pooled claim (almost all neurons <0.5). Semi-matching is computed over weight columns restricted to shared features, not activations. Superposition is induced by design, so the rows bear on V3 only loosely.

statements.correction: Toy models with F=64 features and N=8, 16 or 32 neurons, trained from different seeds: shared features (multiplied norms >=1) are arranged differently across neurons. The text says almost all neurons have a max semi-matching correlation <0.5.
statements.problem: Matches the text. The toy models are built to superpose (N<F, sparse features), and the seeds differ only in initialization.

reader_labels.reason: Across the toy-model sizes, nearly all neurons have maximum semi-matching correlation below 0.5 for shared features across seeds, consistent with shared sparse features being arranged differently across limited neuron populations (r1–r3).
